I stopped four days later. Not that night — I want to be accurate, because the version where a man has a revelation and never smokes again is a lie that makes it harder for everyone who tries it. It took four more days and one more failed morning. What was different this time was that I finally told somebody the true reason. I'd always said I was quitting for my health, because that's what you say. This time I told Marie: I don't want to keep leaving the room. And saying the real reason out loud is what made it stick, because a reason you've said out loud is much harder to negotiate with at half past ten at night.

I used the patches again, and I'll say plainly they helped and I should have used them properly the other eleven times instead of half-using them and blaming them. I moved the chair. That sounds daft. I physically took that chair to the tip, because it was not a chair to me, it was an appointment, and I was not going to sit in the appointment and expect to be fine.

The first fortnight was as bad as everyone tells you. What nobody told me was the third month, when the physical part is long gone and you just feel oddly bereaved. I missed it like you'd miss somebody. I told a mate that and he laughed, and then he said, quieter, that he knew exactly what I meant.

I filled the times, because the times were the problem, not the tobacco. First coffee — I took it out to the garden and stood there like a fool with nothing in my hand until standing there was just standing there. The truck — I put the radio on a talk station because music let me drift and drifting took me straight back. The top field with the view — I kept going. I sat there with a flask and looked at the valley. That one I refused to give up, because it was mine before it was ever the cigarette's.

Where I stand now. Four years in November. I have two grandchildren and I have never once been outside while they were inside. My breathing came back further than I expected, which the doctor said would happen and I hadn't believed. Marie says I'm more here, and she doesn't mean healthier, she means present, and she is right, and it took me a while to stop being defensive about what that says about the previous three decades.

But I'll be straight with you about the daily part, because this is where I think people get let down. Four years and there are still moments. Not cravings the way they were. More like a shape in the corner of the day. A funeral last spring, standing outside the crematorium with people I hadn't seen in years, and half of them smoking, and something in me leaned toward it so hard I had to put my hands in my pockets. It passed in ninety seconds. It always passes in about ninety seconds, and knowing that number is worth more to me than any amount of willpower.

If you're where I was — with your good filing system, knowing everything and doing nothing — I'm not going to lecture you, because eleven failed attempts taught me that lecturing does nothing at all. I'll just say this. Have a look at what it actually costs you, and I don't mean money and I don't mean lungs. Look at where you go when you go for one. Look at what's happening in the room you just left.

I sat outside a lit window for thirty-one years thinking I was having a smoke. I wasn't. I was missing my own life in ten-minute pieces, and there is no version of someday that gives those back. There's just whichever day you decide is day one. Mine was four days after a kitchen full of people I loved. Yours can be a lot sooner than that.

stories.title: Something in My Hand
stories.text:
My name is Tasha, I'm twenty-six, and I vaped for about four years. I'm telling this one because when I was looking for help there was nothing that sounded like me. Everything was written for people who'd smoked for thirty years, and I kept thinking, well, that's not me, I never even smoked. Which turned out to be exactly the thought that kept me in it.

I never smoked a cigarette in my life. Not one. I want that on the record because it's the thing that let me not take this seriously for years. I started vaping at twenty-two, in a flat share, because my flatmate had one and it was mango and it was a laugh. That's the whole origin story. There's no trauma in it. Sometimes there isn't.

By twenty-three it was in my hand constantly. And I do mean constantly — that's the part that's different from cigarettes, and it's the part nobody warned me about. My nan smoked, and my nan had twenty a day and twenty moments a day. I didn't have moments. I had one long continuous moment that started when I woke up and stopped when I fell asleep, and I was topping up my blood every ten minutes without ever once making a decision to.

I worked in a dental practice on reception, which is funny in a bleak way. I'd be on the desk and I'd have it in the drawer, and I'd take a pull between patients, in the toilets, in the car park, in the car at every red light. In bed. That's the one that shames me most. Last thing at night, propped on an elbow in the dark, and first thing in the morning before I'd even properly opened my eyes. That's not a habit. I don't know what that is, but it isn't a habit.

The slide was invisible because there was nothing to see. No smell. No ash. No yellow fingers, no bins full of stubs, none of the evidence that makes a smoker eventually confront themselves. My whole life looked completely normal from the outside, including to me. I upgraded devices twice, went up in strength once without noticing I'd done it, and told myself and everyone else that I was going to stop soon, and I fully believed that sentence every single time I said it.

What it actually took from me is hard to explain because it's all small. I couldn't sit through a film. I genuinely couldn't — I'd be up at some point, out to the hall, and back. I couldn't do a long train journey without planning it around where I could go. I stopped going to my friend Priya's because she had a baby and I wasn't going to vape in there and I couldn't work out how to just be somewhere for four hours. So I saw less of her, and then less, and I told myself we'd both got busy.

My chest got tight in a way I decided was anxiety. Maybe it was. I'll never know now, and honestly not knowing is its own small punishment.

The moment it broke open was so stupid. I've never known how to tell it in a way that sounds like it mattered.

I was at my cousin's wedding. Beautiful day, everyone in the garden, and the speeches started. My uncle got up to talk about his daughter and he was doing that thing where a big gruff man cries, and everyone had gone quiet and warm, and I realised I hadn't had a pull for about twenty minutes and I could not hear a word he was saying. I was standing in the middle of the best moment of that whole family's year, and my entire brain was a flat, whining note about where my bag was.

I went and stood by the bins behind the marquee and had a vape and came back, and I'd missed the end of it. Everyone was clapping. I clapped.

Nobody knew. That's the thing. Nobody saw anything. There was no dramatic scene, no one confronted me, my life carried on being completely fine on the outside. I just stood there clapping for a speech I hadn't heard, and something in me went: you are twenty-six and you are being told what to do by a plastic tube, and you have never once looked at that directly.

I stopped a week later. I'd love to say I did it properly and calmly. I didn't. I threw the thing in a bin outside a Co-op, on impulse, feeling brave, and then had about four hours of feeling brave followed by two days of feeling like I'd been unplugged. I bought another one on day three. That is what happened. I don't skip it, because if you're listening and you've done that, I need you to know that buying another one isn't the end of your attempt, it's just the middle of it.

The second go was less noble and much more effective. I told people, which I'd been too embarrassed to do — because there's a stupid pride in it, isn't there, admitting you're addicted to something you thought was harmless. I told my mum and I told the girls at work and I told Priya, who I'd stopped seeing, and telling Priya was the one that mattered, because she said, very gently, that she'd wondered.

I went down in strength for three weeks instead of stopping dead, which for me was the difference between white-knuckling and actually getting through. I stopped taking my bag to rooms I could do without it in. I learned that the urge lasts about two minutes if you don't feed it and about all day if you do. I took up an absolutely ridiculous amount of chewing gum and I'm not going to pretend that's elegant.

The hardest bit wasn't the nicotine. It was having nothing in my hand. Four years of always having something in my hand, and suddenly my hands were just there, at the ends of my arms, useless. I don't have a clever answer for that. It got better in about six weeks.

Where I am now: fourteen months. I can sit through a film. I sat through a four-hour train to Glasgow reading a book like a normal person and I nearly texted someone about it. I see Priya every week and I hold the baby, and I'm the one who's there for a whole afternoon.

I'll be honest about what's still true. I think about it when I drink. Not badly, but it's there, and I've stopped pretending it won't be. And I get a genuine flare of it when I'm stressed at work, which tells me something about what I was using it for that I hadn't wanted to look at. I'm looking at it now.

If you're my age and you're listening to this thinking it's not that deep because it's only vaping — that was my exact sentence. That sentence cost me four years. It's not that it's dangerous, necessarily, and I'm not the person to tell you what it does to your lungs. It's that it takes your attention, all day, every day, in pieces so small you never notice them going.

I missed my uncle's speech. That's the whole thing. I was there, and I missed it, and there is no way to go back and hear it.

You don't need a rock bottom. There isn't one coming — that's the trap with this stuff, it's too quiet to ever bottom out. You just need one day where you decide the tube doesn't get to hold your attention any more. Mine was a Tuesday, next to a bin, outside a Co-op. It really can be that ordinary.

stories.title: The Second Monitor
stories.text:
My name is Eli. I lost about six years to gaming, and the reason I want to tell it properly is that everyone thinks this story is about a teenager in a basement, and I was thirty-four with a mortgage and a job in logistics.

Before it took hold I was fine. Not thriving, but fine. I'd played games since I was a kid the way most people my age did — a few hours at the weekend, nothing anybody would look at twice. I had a girlfriend, Steph, we'd been together five years, we had a flat with a spare room that was supposed to become something and never did.

What changed wasn't the games. It was 2021, and I was working from home, and I was miserable in a way I couldn't name and definitely wasn't going to talk about. My dad had died the year before and I'd handled it, by which I mean I'd gone back to work eight days later and never mentioned it again. And the game was there, and the game was the only place where I knew exactly what I was supposed to do next.

That's the thing about it that I've never heard anyone say properly. It isn't fun, not by the end. It's legible. Real life at thirty-four is a fog — am I doing well, am I behind, is this the job I'm meant to have, why does everyone else seem to have a plan. In there, there's a bar, and the bar fills, and when it's full you did it right. I wasn't chasing enjoyment. I was chasing being told I'd done something correctly.

The slide had stages and I can see all of them now. First it was after work. Then it was after work until two. Then I started calling in sick, not often, once a month maybe, and I'd tell myself I genuinely felt rough, and part of me believed it. I got a second monitor. I told Steph it was for work. It was not for work.

I stopped answering my mum. She'd ring on Sundays and I'd let it go and text later saying sorry, mad day. My dad's brother tried to take me out for a pint about four times and I cancelled all four. I put on about three stone. My sleep completely inverted — I was going to bed at five and getting up at eleven and doing my job in a kind of grey underwater state where I was technically present and achieving almost nothing.

And Steph. Steph was in the next room. That's what I find hardest to say. Not that she left — she did, eventually, and she was right to. It's that for about two years she was thirty feet away, on a sofa, on her own, every single night, and I knew, and I kept the headphones on. She'd come in and stand in the doorway and I'd do that thing of half taking one ear off, and she learned what that meant, and after a while she stopped coming in.

The moment it broke open. She'd been gone about four months. I want to be clear that her leaving didn't do it — I'd like to say it did, but the honest truth is that when she left, my first feeling underneath the misery was relief, because now nobody was standing in the doorway. That's how far gone I was, and I've had to sit with that.

What did it was a Tuesday afternoon in March. There was a raid, a big one, a guild thing we'd been organising for weeks, and I'd taken the day off for it. Genuinely booked annual leave. And it went well. We cleared it. Everyone was buzzing on voice chat, and this lad from Manchester who I'd never met was shouting, and I felt that lift, that proper hit of it.

And then it ended, and everyone logged off, and it was ten past four in the afternoon on a bright day. And I took the headphones off and the flat was completely silent. And I could hear kids on the green outside coming back from school.

I sat there and I thought: that was the best thing that's happened to me in a year, and it took four hours, and it's over, and there is nothing left of it. Nothing I can show anyone. Nothing that will still be there tomorrow. My dad had been dead two years and I hadn't cried once and I was crying about a video game, except I wasn't, obviously.

I rang my mum. First proper call in about eight months. I didn't tell her any of this, I just asked how she was and let her talk for forty minutes. Then I rang my uncle and said yes to the pint, four cancellations later.

Getting out of it was slower than any of the drinking stories I'd read, and I think that's because there was nothing to abstain from in a clean way. I couldn't just never touch a computer — I work on one. So it wasn't a line, it was a renovation.

I uninstalled the big one. Not all games, the one. I know some people need to go to zero and I respect that, but for me the honest thing was that one specific game had a hook in me — the daily reset, the guild, the obligation, that's what it was, an obligation dressed as a hobby.

The second monitor went. Sold it. That was harder than uninstalling.

I moved my desk. This sounds like nothing and it was the single most effective thing I did. It had been in the spare room with the door shut. I put it in the corner of the front room, in the light, where anybody walking past the window could see me. It's very hard to lose eleven hours in a room you can be seen in.

I got help for the actual problem, which was not gaming. Took me another year to do that. Bereavement counselling through the GP, eight sessions, and I sat in the first one and said I was there about my gaming and the woman let me say that for about twenty minutes and then asked when my father had died. I cried for the rest of the session. Six years of nights in a dark room, and underneath it was one thing I hadn't been able to look at.

Where I am now: two and a half years since that Tuesday. I play maybe four or five hours a week, on the weekend, and I've learned which games are fine for me and which ones aren't, and the difference is whether it punishes you for not showing up. Anything with a daily reset, I don't go near. That's my line and it's specific and it works.

I lost three stone, mostly by accident. I see my mum every fortnight. Steph and I are not together and won't be, and that is a real cost that I don't get to talk my way out of. She was in the next room for two years.

If you're in it — and you'll know, because you'll have felt something tighten when I mentioned the daily reset — I'd say only this. Ask yourself what you knew how to do in there that you didn't know how to do out here. That's the actual question. For me it was: I knew how to be sure I'd done something right. Once I could say that sentence, the game stopped being the enemy and started being a symptom, and symptoms are much easier to deal with than enemies.

Someday, I'd have got round to it. That's what I said for six years, in a dark room with the door shut. Day one was ten past four on a Tuesday afternoon, with kids outside coming home from school, and me finally hearing them.

stories.title: The Envelope in the Drawer
stories.text:
My name is Dean. My wife has a spending addiction, and I want to talk about being the one standing next to it, because I could not find a single thing written for me when I needed it.

We've been married nineteen years. Her name isn't going in this. I'll say she is funny and generous and the person everybody wants at the table, and none of what I'm about to describe cancels that out — I have to say that first, because for about three years I forgot it, and forgetting it did more damage to us than the money ever did.

I'm a heating engineer. Practical man, sensible with money, the sort who reads the meter. So when it started I did what a practical man does, which is treat it as a maths problem. And treating it as a maths problem cost us two years.

It began small and it began after her mother died. I know that now. I didn't then. Parcels, a few a week, nothing outrageous. Clothes mostly, then homeware, then things for the kids that they didn't need and half of which never came out of the packaging. I made jokes about it. Actual jokes, at dinner, in front of people. That's one I'd take back.

The slide, from where I was standing, looked like this. First there was a card I didn't know about. I found the statement and I did the thing I'd do at work: laid it out, went through it line by line, worked out the shortfall, and presented it to her like a survey report. Calm, reasonable, spreadsheet on the table. I genuinely thought I was being good about it. What I was actually doing was showing my wife a list of her worst nights and asking her to explain herself.

She was ashamed and she promised, and she meant it, and for six weeks it stopped. Then it started again with a card I found four months later.

That was the pattern for two years. Discovery, spreadsheet, promise, quiet spell, discovery. And every cycle I got harder and she got better at hiding it. I put us on a joint account. She opened another. I set up alerts. She started paying for things in ways the alerts didn't catch. I want to say clearly to anyone doing what I did: every single control I built, she went round, and every one made her more alone with it, and I could not see that at the time because I was busy being right.

The lowest I got was not about money. I started checking her phone. I'm not proud of it, I did it for months, and I found nothing except order confirmations, which somehow made it worse, because I'd become a man who searched his wife's phone and I hadn't even got the dignity of a reason.

Where it broke open, for me, was an envelope in the drawer of the spare room.

I was looking for a screwdriver. It was one of those thick envelopes and it was full of receipts — not statements, receipts, the little paper ones — going back months. And underneath them, a page from a notepad where she'd written down amounts in a column and totalled them at the bottom and then written the same total again underneath, and circled it. Just that. No note, no letter, nothing to me. Just a woman sitting alone in the spare room adding up what she'd done and circling the number.

I sat on the floor of that room for a long time. Because I had a spreadsheet too. Mine was on the laptop and it was neater. And I understood, sitting there, that we had both been doing the exact same thing in two different rooms for two years — totalling it up in private and not saying a word to each other — and I'd been calling mine responsible and hers a problem.

That was the day I stopped being the auditor.

What changed after that, honestly, because I think this is where people want the practical part.

I stopped presenting evidence. Completely. I never did another spreadsheet-on-the-table conversation. When something came up I'd say one thing, once, about how it made me feel, and then I'd stop talking. That was excruciating for a man like me. Stopping talking felt like letting it win. It wasn't.

I asked one question I had never asked in two years, which was what it felt like in the ten minutes before she bought something. Not why. What it felt like. And she told me, and it took about an hour, and it had nothing to do with things. It was about her mother, and about being twelve, and about a feeling of being about to disappear that buying something interrupted for around twenty minutes. Two years of forensics and I'd never once asked the only question that mattered.

She got proper help. That was hers to do and I want to be careful not to take credit for it. What I did was stop making it harder.

We did do practical things, but we did them together and after that conversation, not as controls imposed on her. She asked me to take her name off two accounts — she asked. We built a spending plan with money in it for things she just wanted, no justification needed, because a plan with no joy in it is a plan you lie about. There's a rule now that anything over a certain figure we say out loud to each other, both of us, and it applies to me too, and that mattered more than I expected.

Where we are now: about three years on. There was a relapse in the second year, a bad month, and here's what was different — she told me. Four days in, she told me, unprompted, and I managed not to become the auditor again, and that is the single thing I'm proudest of in nineteen years of marriage. Not fixing it. Not reacting.

The debt is not gone. We're most of the way and it'll be another two years, and I've stopped treating the finish line as the day I get my wife back, because I already have her.

What I'd say to you, if you're the one standing next to this.

You will want to solve it, because it presents as a money problem and you know how money works. It is not a money problem. The money is the smoke.

Every control you put in place without her will push her further into the room where she does it alone. I built five. All five made it worse.

And watch what you're becoming. I checked my wife's phone for months. I made jokes about her at dinner parties. Nobody warns you that this thing has a second casualty and that you can turn into someone you don't recognise while you're busy being the sensible one.

There was an envelope in a drawer with a number circled on a page, and there was a spreadsheet on my laptop, and they were the same document. We just weren't showing them to each other. The day we did was the day it started getting better — and that day was available for two years before either of us took it.

stories.title: The Blue Light Under the Door
stories.text:
My name is Nadia and my daughter disappeared into her phone for two years while she was standing right in front of me. She's nineteen now and she's all right, and I'm telling this because when I was in it I could not find one person talking about it who wasn't either panicking or telling me it was normal.

Her name is Sana. She was fifteen when it started and she had been, up to then, an easy child in the way that makes you complacent. Drama club. A best friend called Rhi she'd known since she was six. Loud in the house, always singing something.

I'm a district nurse, so I've spent twenty years watching for signs in other people's families. I want you to know that, because it makes what I missed worse and also makes me think anybody can miss it.

It started properly in lockdown, like it did for a lot of them, and that's the excuse I let myself use for far too long. Of course she's on it, everyone's on it, there's nothing else. Then the world opened back up and everyone else came out and she didn't.

The change was so gradual that I kept resetting my sense of normal. She stopped drama. She said it was cringe. Rhi stopped coming round, and when I asked, Sana said they were still friends, which was true in the sense that they still commented on each other's things. She stopped eating with us. Not dramatically — she'd take her plate up, and I let her, and then that was just what happened, and I could not tell you which week it became permanent.

She was on it from waking to sleeping. I'd go past her door at one, at two, and there'd be that blue light under it. I'd knock and say it's late, love, and she'd say I know, and nothing would change. She started looking grey. Her posture went. She got very interested in her face in a way that wasn't vanity, it was more like inspection, and she started saying things about herself that I could not trace to anything real.

The worst of it — and this is the bit I've never been able to say out loud to family — was that she got funnier and cleverer online and quieter and flatter at home. She had a whole self somewhere I couldn't see, and the version I got was the exhausted one at the end of it.

What I did wrong, in order.

I took the phone. Of course I did. Confiscated it for a week when she was sixteen, and I have never seen a human being like it. Not a tantrum. Something closer to grief, and then a kind of blank cold that lasted the whole week and about a fortnight after. And when she got it back she went in twice as deep and, crucially, she got much better at hiding it from me.

I lectured. I sent her articles. God help me, I sent my sixteen-year-old daughter articles about screen time.

I made it a rules problem. Router off at eleven. She had data. Phone charges downstairs. She had an old one. Every rule I made without her, she went round, and every rule taught her that I was somebody to be managed rather than talked to.

And I said the thing that I'd take back before any of the rest. I said, in a bad moment, "You're addicted to that thing," in the tone you'd use about something disgusting. And her face closed, and it stayed closed for about six months.

The moment it turned wasn't a crisis. There was no self-harm, no police, none of the things I'd been braced for. It was a Sunday and I was doing the ironing and she came down for a glass of water, and she stood in the kitchen doorway and said, very flatly, not looking at me: "I don't think I like it any more. I just don't know how to not."

And every instinct in me wanted to say right, brilliant, let's get rid of it, let's do a detox, let's make a plan. Twenty years of nursing and I nearly did the thing you must never do, which is take somebody's first honest sentence and immediately turn it into a treatment plan.

What I actually said, because something stopped me, was: "That sounds exhausting."

And she cried. First time in about a year. And then she talked for an hour and a half, and I found out things about what her days had actually been like that I had no idea about — the counting, the checking, the specific dread of putting something up and watching it not do well, the way she'd started to feel about her own face. None of which had ever come up in eighteen months of me confiscating and lecturing and sending articles.

What worked, after that. And I want to be careful, because a lot of it was hers, not mine.

I stopped policing and started asking. Not about the phone — about the feeling. "What was it like today?" not "How long were you on it?"

She set her own limits, and they were stricter than mine had been, and she broke them, and I didn't say I told you so, and she set them again.

We changed one thing physically and it was the only rule that survived: nothing charges in bedrooms. Mine included. Her father's included. It only worked because it applied to all of us, and honestly, my own evenings got better.

She went back to drama, about eight months later, and that did more than anything I did. It was the first thing in two years she was good at where the feedback wasn't a number.

She saw someone. Six sessions through the school. She hated the first two.

Where we are now. She's nineteen, she's at college doing something creative, she still uses all of it and I've made my peace with that because the goal was never abstinence, it was that she should be the one holding it. She deleted one app entirely last year, by herself, without telling me, and mentioned it a month later like it was nothing.

She and Rhi are friends again. That took a year.

What I'd say to you, if you're a parent listening to this at eleven at night having just walked past a door with blue light under it.

Don't take the phone. Or rather — know what taking it does. It doesn't remove the thing, it removes you from it, and then you're outside and she's inside and there's no door.

Don't use the word addicted at her. Use it in your own head if it helps you take it seriously. Don't say it in that voice. It closed my daughter's face for six months.

Ask what it feels like, not how long she's been on it. One is an interest in her. The other is an audit.

And this one I really mean: watch for the moment she says something true, because it will be small and flat and in a doorway and you will almost certainly be in the middle of something else. Mine was eleven words while I was ironing. If I'd answered that with a plan instead of a sentence, I don't know how long it would have taken to come round again.

She said she didn't know how to not. And it turned out she didn't need me to know either. She just needed me to stop being one more thing in the room she had to manage.

stories.title: The Room I Kept Shut
stories.text:
My name is Brenda. I ran up about forty-one thousand pounds of debt buying things I did not want, and I'd like to explain how a sensible fifty-two-year-old woman does that, because I could not have explained it at the time.

I was a school administrator for twenty-six years. Ran the office. If you'd asked anybody who worked with me they'd have said Brenda's the organised one. I did the rotas. I chased the invoices. I had a label maker and I used it. That woman and the woman I'm describing are the same woman and I've had to make peace with that.

It started after my divorce, when I was forty-four. Not immediately — about a year after, when the noise of it had died down and the house had gone quiet in a way I hadn't been ready for. My son had gone to university. I'd spent twenty years being needed at high volume and then I was in a three-bedroom house on a Tuesday evening with nothing that required me.

The first thing I remember buying was a set of copper pans. I didn't cook, particularly. But there was that hour between ordering them and going to bed where the house felt different. And then there was the tracking, which I'd genuinely look forward to, and then the knock at the door, which is the bit I'd build the whole day around.

Here's what nobody understands who hasn't done it: it was never about owning the pans. I barely used them. It was about the twenty minutes of being someone who had something coming.

The slide took about six years and it was completely invisible because it looked like normal life. A parcel is not a syringe. A parcel is a thing everybody gets. I could buy something on a Tuesday night on my sofa in my dressing gown and there was no bar to walk into, no one to see me, and no point at which anybody could say, Brenda, that's four this week.

The credit was the accelerator. Three cards, then a fourth I opened specifically because the others were near their limit, and I want to be honest about the moment I did that, because that's the moment I'd point at now. I sat at my kitchen table and filled in an application for a card I knew I could not afford, and I had a very clear thought which was: I am doing something wrong here. And I did it anyway, and then I never let myself have that thought again for four years. You can decide not to think something. I'd never known that before.

The spare room filled up. Actually filled — I'd get things and not open them and put them in there, and then I stopped going in there, and then I kept the door shut, and by the end there was a path from the door to the window and nothing else. Two hundred and something pounds of candles. A sewing machine still boxed. Clothes with tags on in sizes I'd never been.

What it cost me. My son stopped being able to stay when he visited, because the room was the room, and I told him the boiler was being done. That lie lasted two years and I still don't know if he believed it. I stopped having anyone in the house at all. I'd meet friends out, always out, and I'd say the place was a tip because of decorating. I lied constantly and easily about very small things and I'd always thought of myself as an honest person.

And the money, obviously. Minimum payments on four cards eats a wage. I was doing sums at three in the morning that never came out and then buying something at seven the next evening.

The moment it broke open was my son, Callum, and it wasn't a confrontation. He came at Christmas and I'd cleared the front room and the kitchen and done the whole performance. And on Boxing Day morning I came down and he was standing in the hall with the spare room door open. He'd gone looking for the ironing board.

He didn't say anything. That's what did it. He looked at it, and he looked at me, and he closed the door, gently, and he said, "Do you want a cup of tea?"

And I said yes, and we had a cup of tea, and he didn't ask, and I understood that my child had just decided to protect me, and that he'd probably been deciding that for a while.

I told him everything that afternoon. All four cards. The number, which I had never said out loud to another human being and had barely said to myself. Forty-one thousand and something. He didn't flinch, he just got a pen.

What actually helped, and I'll be plain because this is the part I needed and couldn't find.

I told somebody the true number. Not a rounded-down number. The real one. I'd been carrying it like a stone and saying it out loud took about a third of the weight off in one go, which I did not expect and cannot explain.

I got proper debt advice, free, from a charity, and I should have done it four years earlier. The plan they built was less frightening than the thing in my head had been. Almost always is, they told me.

I stopped the mechanism, not just the spending. Cards cut up, obviously, but more than that — saved card details deleted from everything, the apps off the phone, and I unsubscribed from every marketing email I had, which took an entire Sunday and which I think was as important as anything else. I could not white-knuckle past a sale email arriving at eight in the evening. So I stopped them arriving.

I worked out what the twenty minutes was for. Took a counsellor to get me there. It was the knock at the door. Somebody coming to my house, for me, with something for me. That's it. That's the whole of it. A woman on her own in a quiet house had found a way to make somebody knock.

So I had to get actual knocks. I joined a choir, which I'd have found mortifying two years earlier. I started having Sunday lunch at my sister's every week whether I felt like it or not.

The spare room took eleven days. Callum came for a weekend and we did it together and about half of it went to charity with the tags still on. I sat on the floor at one point and cried about a boxed sewing machine, and he made tea and let me.

Where I am now. Four years. The debt will be clear in about fourteen months. I still get the pull, and it is very specific — Sunday evenings, and any evening after something's gone wrong. I've stopped being surprised by it.

If you're listening and there's a room in your house you keep shut, or a drawer, or a number you've never said out loud — start with the number. Say it to one person. Not to fix it. Just to stop being the only one carrying it.

I sat in a house full of unopened boxes because I'd found a way to make someone come to the door. It took my son closing that door without a word to show me I'd had a much better way of doing that all along, and his phone number was in my hand the whole time.

stories.title: The Man Who Was Always Almost Home
stories.text:
My name is Victor and I was addicted to work for about twenty years. I know how that sounds. I know that of everything in this app, this is the one people roll their eyes at, and I rolled my eyes at it too, right up until my body stopped and made the decision for me.

I ran operations for a distribution company. Started on the floor at nineteen, ended up running three sites. And I was good — that's the trap, that's what makes this one different from the others. Nobody takes you aside about a habit that keeps getting you promoted.

My wife is called Ines. Two boys, Mateo and Danny. We had a decent house, decent cars, holidays we booked and then I'd cut short. I was, by every measure I understood at the time, providing.

The slide is hard to describe because there wasn't one. It was more that the line kept moving and I moved with it. Sixty hours became seventy. The phone came to the table, then to bed, then on holiday. I answered emails at my nan's funeral — I want to put that in, because I've never said it to anyone and it's the truest single sentence about who I was.

I was never off. That's the thing. Not once, in about fifteen years, was I actually off. Even on the good days, sitting in the garden with a beer, some part of me was running the Monday. My body was in a deckchair and I was in a warehouse in Rugby.

And here's what I told myself, and it was airtight: I'm doing this for them. That sentence is the strongest drug I have ever taken. You cannot argue with a man who is destroying his family for his family. I certainly couldn't.

What it took. Mateo's football, all of it, every Saturday for six years — I went to maybe four. Danny's whole primary school. Ines stopped telling me about things in advance because she'd stopped expecting me and she'd got tired of the disappointment of asking. That's the part I can't get back, that she stopped asking. By the end she'd tell me about parents' evening afterwards, as information.

I want to say what I was actually getting, because it's the same as any of these. At work I was certain. I knew what a good day was. There was a number at the end of the week and if the number was good I'd done well. At home I had no idea if I was doing well. Nobody hands you a number for being a father. So I went where the numbers were and I called it duty.

The moment it broke open was in a car park in Coventry, at ten past seven on a Thursday evening in October, and it was my heart. Not a heart attack, as it turned out — atrial fibrillation, which I now know a lot about. But at the time I was forty-seven years old on my knees between two vans, absolutely certain I was dying, and thinking one thing, over and over, with total clarity.

I was not thinking about my family. That's what I have to tell you. I want to say I was, it would be a better story. I was thinking: the audit's on Tuesday and nobody else knows the system.

Forty-seven, on the tarmac, possibly dying, worrying about an audit.

They kept me in overnight. Ines came, and the boys came in the morning, and Mateo was sixteen and he stood at the end of the bed with his hands in his pockets and he could not look at me. And I thought he was frightened. He wasn't. I found out about six months later, from Ines, that what he'd actually said in the car on the way home was: "He's not going to change though, is he."

Sixteen years old and already retired from hoping about his father.

I'd love to tell you I changed the next week. I went back after eleven days and did four more months, slightly less, telling everyone I'd learned my lesson. What actually changed it was that Ines told me, in February, very calmly, without drama, that she wasn't leaving but she had stopped waiting. She said: "I've built a life that works whether you're in it or not, because I had to. If you want to be in it you'll have to ask."

That was worse than her leaving. And it was the most useful thing anybody has ever said to me.

What I did, practically, because I know that's what you want if you're in this.

I got a diagnosis and took the medication and that was the easy part.

I stepped down. Not out — down. I gave up the third site and took the pay cut, and I want to be honest that this was financially fine and I'd been pretending for years that it wouldn't be. The money was never the reason. I'd been using the money as the reason.

The phone charges in the kitchen from seven o'clock. That's a small rule and it took me about eight months to actually keep it.

I had to learn to be bored, and I was genuinely bad at it. The first few Saturdays with nothing to do I was climbing the walls, and I understood then that I hadn't been working, I'd been medicating. Take the work away and I was left with a level of restlessness that told me something I hadn't wanted to know.

And I had to ask. That's the one. Ines said I'd have to ask to be in the life she'd built, and she meant it, and it was humbling in a way I'd never been humbled. I had to say, can I come. To my own family. For about a year I had to say, can I come, and sometimes the answer was that it was already arranged, and I had to take that on the chin.

Where I am now. Six years. My heart's stable. I work about fifty hours, which some people would say is still too many and I'd say is honest — I'm not going to pretend I became a different man. I went to every one of Danny's last two seasons. Mateo is twenty-two and he rings me, and I don't take that lightly, because there was a year when I don't think he'd have bothered.

Ines and I are better than we were at thirty. Genuinely. It cost us both something to get here and neither of us pretends otherwise.

If you're listening to this on a Sunday night with your laptop open and everyone else in the house asleep, and you're thinking this doesn't apply because your work is real and important and other people depend on you — I know. Mine was too. It was all true. It was true and it was also the thing I was using, and both of those can be true at once, and that's the trap this particular one sets.

Ask yourself one question, and it's the one that got me: when was the last time you were completely off? Not on holiday. Off. If you have to think about it for more than about four seconds, you already know.

There's a version of me that made it to sixty having provided beautifully for a family that had learned to run without him. That man was on the tarmac in Coventry, and the audit was on Tuesday, and nobody else knew the system. Day one was five months later, in a kitchen, being told I'd have to ask.

stories.title: The Light Under the Spare Room Door
stories.text:
My name is Priya. My husband was lost to gaming for about four years while sleeping in the same house as me, and I want to talk about what it's like to be the person on the sofa, because there's very little out there for us and I nearly went under.

We'd been together nine years when it took hold, married for five. He's called Tom and he is, underneath all of this, one of the kindest people I know. I need to say that at the start because for about two years I genuinely stopped being able to see it.

It came on after he was made redundant. He got another job within three months, so we never called it a crisis, but something had gone out of him in those three months that didn't come back. He'd always played a bit. Then he was playing every evening. Then he was playing every evening until three or four in the morning, and getting up at seven, and doing a job he was quietly failing at.

I'm going to describe the specific loneliness of this, because I don't think people understand it. He was thirty feet away. Every night. I could hear him — not the game, the headphones took care of that, but his voice, talking to people I'd never met, laughing at things I wasn't in. I'd be on the sofa with the telly on low, listening to my husband have a good time with strangers through a wall.

I'd go in. I'd stand in the doorway and he'd lift one side of the headphones off and look at me with this expression of enormous patience, like I was a colleague who'd come to his desk. And I'd say something about bed, and he'd say two minutes, and I'd go, and I'd lie there and hear him still going at one, at two.

After a while I stopped going in. I want anyone listening to notice that, because it's the moment things get properly dangerous and it feels at the time like being reasonable. I stopped going in because I couldn't take the patient face any more. And once I stopped going in we were just two people in a house.

What I tried, and what it did.

I got angry. Big rows, the works, three or four of them a year. They achieved nothing except that afterwards he'd play less for about a week and then more than before, and he'd be careful about it, and careful is worse. Careful means they've started managing you.

I made it about the time. "You were on it till three." Which let him argue about the time — no it was half two, and anyway I was up at seven, and I'm functioning aren't I. And he was, technically, functioning. So I lost every one of those arguments on the facts while being completely right about the thing underneath.

I read about it and I started using language at him. Addiction. Escapism. I sent him a link once. He read it, said it was interesting, and went upstairs.

And this is my confession: I started keeping score. Actually counting nights. I had a note on my phone. I told myself it was so I'd have evidence, and I did eventually put it in front of him, and it did precisely nothing except tell him I'd been watching him for four months.

I also got very small. That's the bit I'd warn people about hardest. I stopped inviting people round because I'd have to explain where he was. I stopped making plans for us because they got cancelled. I got so used to my own company that I started to prefer it, and that frightened me more than anything he was doing.

The thing that changed it wasn't me. I need to be honest about that because I spent two years believing the right sentence existed and I just hadn't found it. There is no sentence. It was his dad's anniversary and something cracked in him on his own, in the afternoon, and he came downstairs and sat on the arm of the sofa and said, "I think I've been hiding."

What I did in that moment was the only genuinely good thing I did in four years, and it was entirely accidental: I said nothing. I had four years of prepared material — I could have said all of it, and it was all true, and I would have been completely justified. And something in me just went quiet and let him keep talking.

He talked for two hours. Most of it wasn't about the game.

What worked afterwards, in case it's useful.

He uninstalled the specific game, not gaming. I'd been demanding total abstinence for years and I was wrong. The problem was one game with a daily obligation in it — he'd describe it as a job he wasn't paid for and couldn't quit.

The desk came out of the spare room and went into the front room. His idea. It changed everything and neither of us has ever fully understood why. Something about not being able to disappear.

He got counselling, about his dad, which was what all of it had actually been about.

And I got something too, and this is the part I'd say to any partner listening. I went to two sessions on my own about what those four years had done to me, because I had genuinely stopped being able to feel much, and I'd have called that coping. It wasn't coping, it was flattening, and it took months to come back from.

Where we are now: two and a half years. He plays at weekends, a few hours, in the front room, and I've had to work at not standing over it like a probation officer. That was harder than I expected. Trusting again is a separate job from him getting better and nobody warns you about that either.

What I'd say to you if you're the one on the sofa.

Standing in the doorway doesn't work and stopping standing in the doorway is worse. I don't have a good answer to that. I only know that the night I stopped going in was the night it got properly bad, and if I could go back I'd keep going in, badly, pointlessly, rather than let the house go quiet.

Don't count. Whatever you're tempted to keep a record of, don't. It turns you into something and it doesn't move them an inch.

Watch what happens to you. Not to them — to you. I got smaller for four years and I called it being patient.

And when they finally say something true, say nothing. I had four years of correct arguments loaded and ready and the best thing I ever did was not fire a single one. He'd been building up to that sentence for a long time, and if I'd met it with my evidence I don't know how long it would have taken him to try again.

stories.title: Fourteen
stories.text:
My name is James and my son started vaping at fourteen. He's seventeen now and he stopped last year, and the reason I'm telling this is that I handled the first eighteen months of it about as badly as a person can, and I'd like somebody else to skip that part.

He's called Rowan. Middle of three. He was the easy one — that's a thing people say and it's usually a warning. Quiet, kind, played bass badly and joyfully, and had the same three friends since primary.

I found out the way most parents do, which is by finding one. In a coat pocket, doing the washing. Small blue thing, blueberry ice.

And I lost my mind. Not shouting exactly — worse, I think. I did the cold, disappointed, sit-down-son version. I told him he was throwing his lungs away. I told him he was being played by a company that wanted him hooked, which is true and which I delivered in a tone that made it about him being stupid rather than about them being predatory. I said, and I'll never lose this one, "I thought you had more sense."

Fourteen years old and I told him he'd disappointed me about a thing he already felt bad about. Everything after that was me trying to get back to the ground I'd given up in that one conversation.

For a year and a half we did the following. I searched. He hid. I found. He got better at hiding. I took his phone off him once because I'd read that they buy them off each other on there, and he didn't speak to me properly for a fortnight. I put a monitoring thing on his laptop and told him I'd done it, thinking honesty made it acceptable. He said, "Right," and went upstairs, and something between us that had been there since he was born went very quiet.

I want to be honest about what was underneath it for me, because it wasn't really his lungs. It was that my dad smoked and died at sixty-one and I watched it, and I was terrified, and I turned my terror into a rule and pointed it at my kid. Fear looks like anger when it comes out of a father.

Meanwhile the thing itself got worse. He went from now and then to constantly. He couldn't sit through a meal. He was up in the night, and I knew he was, because I'd hear the floorboard. He got irritable in a way that wasn't teenage — there's a difference, and by month ten I could tell. He'd come back from being out and be fine, and forty minutes into being at home he'd be snapping at his little sister.

And his mum and I disagreed about all of it, constantly, which is its own thing nobody mentions. She thought I was making it enormous. I thought she was letting it go. We had that argument about thirty times.

The moment it turned was in the car, and I only got it right by accident because I was too tired to do it properly.

Driving him back from his gran's, half nine at night, motorway, dark, both of us looking straight ahead — which I now know is the only way a fifteen-year-old boy will tell you anything. And out of nothing he said, "I've tried to stop, you know."

And I was so tired that instead of my usual material I just said, "How's it gone?"

And he said, "Four days once. It was horrible."

Two and a half years I'd been treating this as defiance. It had never once occurred to me that he'd been trying and failing on his own and hadn't told me, because why on earth would he tell the man who said he thought he had more sense.

I didn't say anything clever. I said, "That sounds rubbish. Do you want a hand?"

He said, "Maybe."

That was the whole conversation. We didn't speak again for the rest of the drive. It was the most productive eleven minutes of the entire three years.

What actually worked after that.

I stopped being the police. Completely. No searching, no pockets, no monitoring. I told him I'd stopped and I meant it, and I think he tested it for about two months before he believed it.

I asked him what it was for. Turned out it was mostly anxiety about school and a bit of not knowing what to do with his hands in social situations, which I recognised immediately because I was exactly the same at that age with cigarettes and had somehow never made the connection.

We got the GP involved, which I'd assumed would be useless and wasn't. He was offered proper support and he took some of it and ignored the rest.

He went down in strength over about six weeks instead of stopping dead, because stopping dead was what he'd tried four times on his own and it had failed four times.

He told his friends he was stopping, which I think did more than everything I did put together.

And I apologised. Properly, once, without a but on the end. For the sense comment, specifically, because I could tell it had lodged. He shrugged it off but he went a bit red, and I knew it had landed.

Where we are now. Fourteen months clear. He's seventeen, he's doing his A-levels, he plays bass slightly less badly. He talks to me, which for a stretch there I didn't think was coming back.

What I'd say to any parent who's just found one in a coat pocket, standing in a utility room deciding what to do.

Your first reaction is the most important thing that will happen in this whole story, and you get about four seconds to choose it. I used mine to tell my son he'd disappointed me, and I paid for that for eighteen months.

Assume he's already tried to stop. Genuinely assume it. Mine had, four times, and never said, because I'd made myself the last person on earth he'd admit a failure to.

Don't search. Everything you find buys you one conversation and costs you a year of him talking to you.

And know what you're actually frightened of. Mine was my father, dead at sixty-one, and my son had nothing to do with it. He just had to stand there and take it.

He's fourteen months clear because one night on a motorway I was too tired to give him the speech, and asked him a question instead. That's it. That's the whole difference between the first eighteen months and the last fourteen.

stories.title: Two Thousand Photographs of a Life I Wasn't In
stories.text:
My name is Lorna, I'm thirty-eight, and I lost about five years to my phone. Not to anything on it particularly. To the checking.

I was a primary school teacher and then I had Iris and went part-time, and the part-time is where it got its teeth into me. Anybody who's been at home with a baby knows about the hours — that stretch between two and five in the afternoon that has no shape to it at all. That's where it started, and I want to be fair to myself: it wasn't a weakness, it was that I was lonely and it was the only door out of the room.

The first year I'd have called it staying connected. And it was, at first. Then somewhere in the second year it stopped being connection and became measurement.

Here's the shape of it, and I've spoken to enough women now to know it's not just me. I'd post something about Iris. Then I'd check. Then I'd check again. And the checking wasn't pleasure, it was more like taking a reading. And the reading was never good enough, and when it was good it was good for about ninety seconds and then I needed another one.

And underneath the checking was the comparing, which is the part that did the real damage. I knew, intellectually, that everyone posts their best. I taught children about that. And it made not the slightest difference, because I wasn't comparing my life to their lives, I was comparing how I felt on the inside to how they looked on the outside, at three in the afternoon, in a dressing gown, with a baby who wouldn't sleep.

What it took from me. Time, obviously, and I'd rather not know the number. But specifically: I stopped reading, entirely, and I'd been someone who read. I stopped ringing my sister, because we messaged and I told myself that was the same. My sleep went, badly, for about three years, because I'd do that thing of putting the phone down and picking it up again eleven times.

And the one I find hardest. I have about two thousand photographs of Iris between one and four, and I was behind the camera for a lot of things I do not actually remember. I remember getting the picture. I remember choosing which one. I do not remember the afternoon. There's a video of her first proper run across a park and I can hear myself in it, going "go on, go on" — and I know from the sound of my own voice that I was watching a screen.

My husband said something once, quite mildly, at about year three. He said, "You're not really here in the evenings." And I was so defensive that he never said it again, and I've thought a lot since about all the things he might have said in the two years after that, if I hadn't taught him what it cost.

The moment it broke open, and it's small.

Iris was four and a half. She was doing a thing with a cardboard box in the front room, some elaborate game, and she'd been narrating it at me for a while. And she stopped and looked over and said, completely without malice, in the tone you'd use about the weather: "You can look at your phone if you want. I don't mind."

She was four. She'd worked out that my attention was a limited resource that she was competing for, and she'd decided, at four years old, to be gracious about losing.

I put the phone face down on the arm of the chair and I said, no, I want to see, and she carried on. And I sat there and watched her and felt sick.

What I did, and I'll be plain about the parts that failed.

I tried deleting the apps first. Lasted nine days. I reinstalled one at eleven at night and told myself it was to check something. So: deleting alone did not work for me, and I don't think it works for most people, because it's a wall with no door in it and you just climb it.

What did work was smaller and more boring.

I put a charging point in the kitchen and the phone lives there. Not at night — all the time, unless I'm taking it somewhere. That single physical change did more than any app blocker.

I turned off every notification except calls and texts from about six people. This took me an hour and I should have done it five years earlier. Nothing on my phone is allowed to start a conversation with me any more. I start them.

I unfollowed about two hundred people, and here's the bit I'd pass on: not the ones I disliked. The ones I compared myself to. Some of them were friends. It was a strange thing to do and it worked immediately.

I put something in the hole. That's the real work. That two-to-five stretch had to become something, so it became a walk, most days, however grim, and about a year later it became a choir, and I'd have laughed at that once.

And I told my husband and my sister what I'd been doing. Actually said it out loud — that I checked my phone a hundred times a day and felt worse every time. My sister said, "Oh thank God," and then told me about hers.

Where I am now. Three years. I use two of them, on a laptop, in the evening, deliberately, for maybe twenty minutes. My phone is a phone. I read about thirty books last year, which I mention only because it was the thing I'd have said was gone forever.

Iris is eight. I have a lot fewer photographs of her between five and eight. I remember all of it.

If you're listening to this while doing the thing — and you probably are, that's not a criticism, that's just how it goes — I'm not going to tell you it's ruining your life, because it isn't necessarily. Mine wasn't ruined. It was thinned. Every day had a bit less in it and I couldn't tell, because the thing taking it was also the thing I was using to check whether I was all right.

Ask one question. Not how long you're on it. Ask what you're checking for. There's an answer under there and it's usually not about the phone at all. Mine was: tell me I'm doing this properly. Nobody was ever going to be able to tell me that, least of all two hundred people I'd chosen because they made me feel behind.

A four-year-old gave me permission to ignore her, kindly, because she'd learned that's how it worked. I'd been telling myself I'd sort it out at some point. That was the point. There isn't a better one coming.
